Process

My process isn’t a straight line. I move between framing, making, testing and refining—using AI to accelerate exploration while keeping product judgment, visual craft and user needs firmly human.

01 / Frame

Frame the right problem

It all starts with understanding the problem we’re trying to solve, who experiences it and why it matters. Before opening Figma—or prompting a model—I define the desired outcome, constraints and assumptions behind the work.

I constantly return to the same question: “What exactly is the problem we’re trying to solve and why?” AI can produce answers quickly, but speed is only useful when we’re asking the right question.

I keep the problem visible by writing it down, mapping what we know and separating evidence from assumption. My sketchbook is still one of my most useful tools for slowing down, thinking clearly and capturing the questions that should guide the work.

02 / Discovery

Research, synthesis
and signal

Research begins with people, behavior and context. I combine customer conversations, product data, competitive analysis and visual research to understand what matters—not just what already exists.

AI helps me organize large amounts of information, cluster recurring themes, summarize competing perspectives and identify questions worth investigating. I treat those outputs as hypotheses, not evidence, and validate them against primary research and real user behavior.

I also collect visual references across products, culture, typography, motion and brand. Inspiration can come from a small interaction detail or an entirely different industry, so I capture broadly before narrowing toward a point of view.

03 / Ideation

Explore broadly

Once the problem is clear, I deliberately create multiple directions before committing to one. I sketch by hand, work through flows in Figma and use generative tools to explore alternate structures, content models, visual languages and edge cases.

AI makes divergence faster. Instead of polishing the first reasonable idea, I can compare more possibilities, challenge familiar patterns and bring stronger options into critique. Direction, taste and the decision about what deserves to move forward remain human responsibilities.

04 / Prototyping

Prototype to learn

Prototypes turn opinions into something observable. Depending on the question, I move between lightweight flows, high-fidelity Figma prototypes and functional coded experiences.

AI helps me generate realistic content, simulate product states and build working experiments earlier in the process. This allows teams to experience an idea—not just discuss it—and uncover interaction, technical and storytelling problems before investing heavily in production.

I keep iterations visible as the work evolves. The progression helps collaborators understand why decisions were made, compare alternatives and give feedback against the original problem rather than personal preference.

05 / Refinement

Validate, refine
and ship

I put prototypes in front of users, stakeholders and engineering partners as early as possible. Feedback is compared against the original problem, not simply incorporated by consensus.

AI can accelerate critique, accessibility reviews, content variations and design-system documentation, but the final decisions remain grounded in user evidence, product strategy and human judgment.

From there, I refine the details, support implementation, learn from the release and feed those lessons back into the next iteration. Shipping is not the end of the process—it is the start of better evidence.
